body.x: Most couples sign the standard nikah contract — the aqd, the mahr, the names and signatures — without realising the contract can carry more. In the Shia tradition, a marriage contract may include stipulations, known as shurut: conditions the couple themselves agree and write into the contract, which then bind both parties as part of the marriage itself. The printed nikah nama already contains a section for conditions; this guide is about what couples actually put there, what makes a condition hold, and how to raise the subject without it sounding like a lack of trust.

Added conditions are usually practical rather than dramatic. They record, in binding form, things the couple have already agreed in conversation and do not want left to memory or goodwill. The subjects that come up most often are these:

Residence: the city or country the couple will live in, or that a move abroad requires both partners' consent
Education and work: that either spouse may continue their studies or their career after marriage
Living arrangements: a home of the couple's own, or a defined period in the family home with a date to review it
Travel and postings: how long stays with family abroad, or work placements in another city, will be decided
Religious life: arrangements that protect both spouses' ability to practise, worship and observe as they should

Notice what these have in common: none of them invents a new right. Each takes an understanding the couple reached while courting and gives it the protection of the contract, so that a promise made in good spirits is still honoured in difficult ones.
The condition people ask about most: delegated authority

One stipulation is asked about more than all the others. Under it, the husband grants his wife a delegated authority — a wakala — under which, if clearly defined circumstances arise, she may set in motion the process of ending the marriage through the proper scholarly and legal channels rather than depending entirely on his cooperation. The circumstances are spelled out in the condition itself, and couples who include it typically name grave situations: abandonment, a failure to provide maintenance, or serious harm. This is not a sentence to improvise. Its validity and exact effect depend on wording, and scholars differ on particular formulations, so it must be drafted with the officiant who will perform the aqd and checked against the guidance of each side's own marja. Done properly, many couples describe it not as a threat but as insurance neither expects to use — and its presence is often what allows a bride's family to proceed with a peaceful heart.

Three things decide whether a condition actually binds. First, it must form part of the contract: stipulations are written into the nikah itself, agreed and recorded at the time of the aqd, not exchanged as side promises afterwards. Second, its subject must be lawful — a condition cannot make something forbidden into something permitted. Third, it must not contradict the essence of marriage itself; a condition that negated the marital relationship altogether, for example, would undermine the very contract it sits inside. Beyond those tests, clarity is everything. A vague condition invites the dispute it was meant to prevent, so each one should say who must do what, by when, and what follows if they do not. Because the application of these tests differs in detail between marjas, the couple's own scholars — not an article — have the final word on any specific wording.
Raising conditions without poisoning the trust

Timing does most of the work. Conditions belong in the conversation weeks before the ceremony, while the match is still being finalised — raised for the first time on the wedding day, even a reasonable one feels like an ambush. Framing does the rest. Present conditions as protection for both sides, because they are: a residence clause protects a husband's career as readily as a wife's studies, and either spouse may propose them. Invite the other family to add conditions of their own, and mean it. Involve the walis and elders as witnesses to the fairness of the exchange rather than as negotiators to be defeated. And apply the symmetry test to every line: would we accept this condition if it were reversed? A condition that survives that question rarely damages trust. One that fails it usually deserves to.
Get the wording drafted, not improvised

Sit with the officiant who will perform the aqd and draft the conditions with him, in writing, before the day. Each side may also consult their own marja's office on wording — a short question asked early is far easier than a dispute unwound later. One further distinction matters. A condition can be religiously binding and yet have limited standing in a civil court, depending on the country; where a condition carries real-world weight — property, residence in another country, a child's schooling — take local legal advice as well, and keep the signed contract with the couple's other marriage documents. Religious validity and civil enforceability are separate questions, and a careful couple answers both.

A condition written calmly before the nikah is not a sign of doubt. It is how two families turn good intentions into something that still protects everyone on a bad day. Start the conversation early, keep it mutual, and let scholars you trust settle the wording. And if you are still at the stage of meeting prospects, the wali-involved process on Shia Rishta gives families a natural setting to raise expectations of every kind — including these — before hearts and dates are fixed.
